doc.title: Terri Lyne Carrington interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Visiting Papa Jo Jones near the end of his life
summary: She taped a conversation with Papa Jo Jones, who felt abandoned; discussion of pensions and his place in jazz history.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Was he — gosh I guess I read near the end of his life he was cantankerous? Is that a fair statement or was he not with you perhaps?

Yeah. Not so much with me. I just found a way to try to pull out the positive energy and you know, him and anybody else that I was around. It’s funny when I listen back to the tape there were definitely some things that were said that I would not have been able to put on the record or really maybe even play for too many people, just, you know, him being a little bitter. You can hear that he was a little bitter, even with what I did put on the record. Because he felt like nobody came to visit him when he was dying. And I had to say, “Well I’m here, and I came to visit you with Max Roach, and I came to visit you I believe with Jack DeJohnette so I know that they came.” And while I was sitting there Billy Higgins called him, while I was doing the interview. I mean well not really an interview, but while I was talking to him and recording. So you know there were people © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

that were there for him but he felt like nobody was there for him. And it was really sad to see how he passed as far as his living conditions. You know he had I think not really a nurse but a careperson coming in maybe once a day. I don’t know how long they stayed but it didn’t seem like a very comfortable situation for him.
That’s part of the business nowadays that I guess has changed for the positive where fellas like him were not putting aside any money and they weren’t getting retirement I suppose.

Yeah the pensions, and I mean unless you were in the union and doing those kinds of — I mean I’m not even sure when the union really got serious about — I’m not sure what years the union got serious about pensions and all that. But unless you’re playing shows or studio work, live gigs aren’t normally like that even today unless you make your own pension or somehow if you do it through a corporation you contribute to your own pension. But people don’t think about all that.
Yeah. How did he feel about his place in jazz history?

You know I’m not sure. I mean I was also very young, I was eighteen I believe when he passed. So that’s actually many years ago. It’s funny my goodness. But I’m not sure. I would never start to try to answer that.
